name: Zoe Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Pryce's orchards, sixty hectares of apples and pears on the slope above the village, for the Pryce family, who've owned it four generations. November is pruning season. I'm out with my team of three by half seven, each of us with a ladder and loppers, working down the rows, and I'm deciding on every tree which branches stay and which go. It's slow work, and it's the work that decides next year's crop.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Blossom week in April. You stand at the top of the slope and the whole valley's white and pink, and the bees are so loud it sounds like an engine. And I like knowing that some of the trees I planted at twenty-five are in their best years now. An orchard teaches you patience whether you want it or not.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Picking season, September and October. Fifteen extra pickers, mostly the same families every year, and the cold store, and the buyer phoning to say the apples are a bit small this year so the price is down. The pay isn't great for what I do, and Graham's work as an electrician comes and goes. We've less than a month saved, so a late frost in May is a frightening thing.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not much, but more than I did. The cold store has sensors. Last year my neighbour showed me how she photographs a sick leaf and an AI tells her what disease it is, and after watching her get it right three times, I started doing the same. I don't use it for much else. I'd rather ask old Bill at the next farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's handy for some things, like the leaf photos, and leave it there. After church, someone would say it's the end of the world, and someone else would say it's marvellous. I'd say it's a tool, like a better pair of loppers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it changes very little. My year is frost, scab, the buyer's price and whether the pickers come back. A cleverer search engine doesn't do anything about those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it a bit more, maybe to check the spray timings and write the reports for the Pryces. Otherwise nothing changes. Prune in winter, thin in summer, pick in autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quietly glad, maybe, if it saves me an evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a late frost in May. What does that do to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four years ago we lost two thirds of the crop in one night. I was up at two lighting the frost candles, the little burners between the rows, with Graham and the kids in their pyjamas helping. We still lost it. The Pryces cut my bonus and we lived on beans and the freezer for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather ask old Bill. Who is he?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bill's eighty-one and he's grown apples on the next farm for sixty years. He can tell a tree's sick from the road. When he goes, a lot goes with him, and no machine has ever met him.

S0.say: I'd say it's handy for some things, like the leaf photos, but it's just a tool, like a better pair of loppers. After church some would call it the end of the world and others marvellous.
S0.think: I think it changes very little, since my year is frost, scab, the buyer's price and whether the pickers return. A cleverer search engine doesn't touch those.
S0.do: Uses AI a little more to check spray timings and write reports for the owners. Otherwise keeps the orchard year as it is: prune in winter, thin in summer, pick in autumn.
S0.feel: Calm, and quietly glad if it saves an evening.
S0.quote: When he goes, a lot goes with him, and no machine has ever met him.
S0.fieldNote: She's steady and practical, and took up AI only after seeing her neighbour get it right three times. The frost night with her family in pyjamas showed exactly how thin her cushion is. She values older knowledge like Bill's highly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the second. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is how it should be, and it gives people time to adjust. But firms not hiring young people is wrong. A young person needs a first job and someone to show them how, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the buyer gets the clever systems first. Pricing, grading, deciding what's too small. They'd squeeze us tighter, and the Pryces would squeeze me. My own work, pruning a tree, that's safe for a long while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever system the buyer makes us use, once the other growers have, and I'd keep my own records so I can argue back. I'd also take on a young person for the pruning season, maybe Bill's grandson, so the knowledge passes on. The Pryces would have to pay him, and I'd make the case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. More for the young ones than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Making the case to the Pryces, how would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Pryce would say yes because his father took on boys. His son, who'll take over, would ask what it costs per tree. I'd have to answer both of them, which is my job really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bill's grandson. Does he want to do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's seventeen and he's not sure. He likes being out, but his mates are all going to the city. I'd tell him the city will always be there, and a good pruner is rarer than a good accountant.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is how it should be, giving people time to adjust. But firms not hiring young people is wrong, because a young person needs a first job and someone to teach them.
S1.think: I think the buyer gets the clever pricing and grading systems first and squeezes us harder, so the owners squeeze me. My pruning work is safe for a long while.
S1.do: Learns the buyer's system once other growers have, keeps her own records to argue back, and makes the case to the owners to take on her neighbour Bill's grandson for the pruning season.
S1.feel: A little uneasy, more for young people than for herself.
S1.quote: I'd tell him the city will always be there, and a good pruner is rarer than a good accountant.
S1.fieldNote: Her traditional values show as passing on skills through people, not systems. She's realistic about juggling the old owner and his cost-minded son. She'd adapt to the buyer's systems, but only after others had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad for the people losing jobs, but the answer is work, not handouts. Let businesses grow and hire, and help people learn a trade. The politicians arguing about it will just make it worse, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's coming closer. Graham does a lot of work for offices in town, rewiring, fitting out. If the offices shrink, so does his work, and he's already quiet some months. That's half our income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Graham to chase work on the new housing estates and farms, not offices. I'd cut back, no holiday this year, and the kids' after-school club, that's about eighty a month. I'd ask the Pryces if I could run a farm stall at the gate, apples and juice, to bring in a bit extra on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and more so than before. I'd be counting more often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the answer's work, not handouts. If Graham couldn't find work, would you take help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go to family first. My brother has the dairy, he'd find Graham something. And the church has a hardship fund that's helped other families. I'd rather that than the government, because they know you and they expect you back on your feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A stall at the gate. Has anyone done that round here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plum farm did, years back. They sold more at the gate on a sunny Sunday than to the buyer in a week, at a better price. It's honest money, people see what they're buying and who grew it.

S2.say: I'd say it's sad for those losing jobs, but the answer is work, not handouts: let businesses hire and help people learn a trade. The arguing politicians will only make it worse.
S2.think: I think it's coming closer because my partner does much of his electrical work for offices in town. If offices shrink so does his work, which is half our income.
S2.do: Urges her partner to chase work on housing estates and farms, drops the family holiday and the eighty-a-month after-school club, and asks the owners to let her run a weekend gate stall for apples and juice.
S2.feel: More uneasy than before, counting money more often.
S2.quote: I'd rather that than the government, because they know you and they expect you back on your feet.
S2.fieldNote: Her preference for family and church help over government came with a clear reason: being known and expected to recover. Her worry has moved to her partner's office-based work. The gate stall idea is small, local and very much her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the fourth. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who saved and invested shouldn't be punished for it. But if the whole country's in a crisis, everyone should pull together, and those who've done very well should give something back, through their churches and charities and businesses, not just tax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think orchard work stays safe for now, but our customers change. When people lose good jobs, they buy cheaper fruit, imported, and our apples go to juice at a third of the price. And house prices going up only helps people who own several houses. Hattie and Sam will never live in this village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with the Pryces early and suggest we plant some cider apple varieties, which sell to the cider makers on long contracts. Steady money, even if the prices are lower. I'd put every spare penny from the gate stall into savings. And I'd talk to Graham about whether he should train in solar panels, since the rich are still building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not my job I'm afraid for, it's the life around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Planting cider apples takes years. Is that realistic when things are moving this fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything in an orchard takes years, that's the point. A tree planted now crops in four. If the world's gone mad, I'd still want something steady growing on that slope. It's the only way I know to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Hattie and Sam will never live in the village. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. My family's been in this parish for generations, there are Quinns in the churchyard back to the eighteen-hundreds. The idea that my children would have to leave to afford a roof, that's the part that keeps me awake.

S3.say: I'd say people who saved and invested shouldn't be punished. But in a national crisis everyone should pull together, and those who've done very well should give back through churches, charities and businesses, not just tax.
S3.think: I think orchard work stays safe for now, but hard-up customers would buy cheap imported fruit, sending our apples to juice at a third of the price. Booming house prices mean my children won't afford to live in the village.
S3.do: Suggests to the owners early on planting cider apples for steady long contracts, saves every spare penny from the gate stall, and talks to her partner about training in solar panel installation.
S3.feel: Anxious, not for her job but for the life around it.
S3.quote: Everything in an orchard takes years, that's the point.
S3.fieldNote: Her answer to a fast-moving crisis was to plant trees that take four years, which says a lot about her. The deepest worry is her children being priced out of a parish her family has lived in for generations. Her politics favour giving back over taxing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're throwing away skills that took generations to build, for the sake of a cheaper apple. I'd say farms should be helped to keep people on, and young people should get apprenticeships, not just be told to learn coding. I'd say it at the growers' association, and probably in the parish newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think picking robots are already being tested in orchards, the ones with suction tubes. Add pruning robots with cameras and the Pryces don't need my team, or the fifteen pickers. They'd need someone to manage the machines, and maybe that's me, if I'm willing. I'm not sure I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see the first orchards that use them, and talk to the managers there before I decided anything. If it worked, I'd ask the Pryces to train me on it, and to keep my team on for the pruning as long as possible. And I'd tell Graham to get into fixing the machines, because they'll all need electricians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like standing in the orchard in May at two in the morning watching the thermometer drop, and there's nothing more you can light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe that's you, if you're willing. What's stopping you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pride, partly. I'm good at something that took me twenty years. And partly I'd feel I'd betrayed my team, Ruth and Tomasz and Dev. But I've got a mortgage and two kids, and pride doesn't pay a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the pickers, the families who come every year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them myself, face to face, the season before. Some of them have been coming for fifteen years, I've watched their children grow up in the photos they show me. I'd want them to hear it from me, not from a letter.

S4.say: I'd say we're throwing away skills built over generations for a cheaper apple. Farms should be helped to keep people on and young people should get apprenticeships, and I'd say it at the growers' association and in the parish newsletter.
S4.think: I think suction picking robots and camera pruning robots would mean the owners no longer need my team or the fifteen pickers. They'd need someone to manage the machines, maybe me if I'm willing, and I'm not sure I am.
S4.do: Waits to see the first orchards using robots and talks to their managers before deciding. If it works, asks the owners for training while keeping her team on pruning, and urges her partner to repair the machines.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like watching the thermometer drop in a May frost with nothing left to light.
S4.quote: Like standing in the orchard in May at two in the morning watching the thermometer drop, and there's nothing more you can light.
S4.fieldNote: She would adapt, but only after seeing proof, and she named pride and loyalty to her team as the brakes. The frost image tied back to the real night she lost the crop. Her wish to tell the pickers face to face showed her sense of duty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, the robots in the orchard. The others I can see a way through, with the stall and the cider apples and Graham's work. That one takes the skill itself. What would help is apprenticeships and support for farms that keep people on, so the knowledge isn't lost, and some help for families like ours with no savings, ideally through people who know us.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the trees. An orchard is planted for the next generation, not this one. If we let it all go to machines and cheap imports, the next lot won't even know what we had. That's what I'd want written down.

headlineQuote: Pride, partly. I'm good at something that took me twenty years. And partly I'd feel I'd betrayed my team, Ruth and Tomasz and Dev.
portrait: Zoe Quinn, 43, runs a sixty-hectare apple and pear orchard for the family that has owned it for four generations, leading a team of three pruners and fifteen seasonal pickers on modest pay with less than a month saved. She is patient, wry and rooted in her parish and church, and she uses AI only for photographing sick leaves, after watching her neighbour prove it worked. She favours work, family and church help over government handouts. Through the scenarios she plans in seasons and years, worrying first about her partner's work and her children being priced out of the village, then about robots that would take the skill itself.
biggestWorry: The robot scenario, because picking and pruning robots would take away the skill itself and the jobs of her team and the pickers.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships and support for farms that keep people on, and help for families with no savings, ideally through people who know them.
